question: The 2011 Istanbul Convention is a key pillar in the fight against gender-based violence, putting the concept of consent at the core of defining the crime of rape. The ‘only yes means yes’ principle, which emphasises the importance of explicit consent in sexual relations, is crucial to protect women’s dignity and rights, by reducing the room for legal ambiguity that can leave perpetrators unpunished.

In the context of the inter-institutional negotiations on the proposal for a directive on combating violence against women and domestic violence, the attempt by some Member States to remove Article 5, which defines the crime of rape on the basis of consent, is a serious case of backsliding on women’s rights and in the fight against gender-based violence. In view of the above: 1.

How will the Commission ensure that the EU’s legal environment around gender-based violence holds onto its crucial advances and does not suffer any weakening that could endanger women’s safety and rights?
What actions can it take to actively promote consent-based legislation at EU level, taking national best practices as examples?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.3.2024) The Commission regrets that the definition of rape, as proposed by the Commission, was not included in the final text of the Directive of the European Parliament and of the Council on combating violence against women and domestic violence1. However, the adoption of the Directive is a big achievement in ensuring women’s safety and rights.

The Directive sets out a range of measures on protection, support and access to justice for victims of violence against women and domestic violence. These measures will benefit victims of all forms of such violence if criminalised at national level, including victims of rape.

The co-legislators also agreed on a strong article on prevention measures related to rape and the central role of consent in sexual relationships. Member States will be required to increase knowledge of the fact that non-consensual sex is considered a criminal offence through awareness campaigns, and to promote the understanding that consent must be given voluntarily as a result of the person’s free will.

This provision will enhance the knowledge in Member States of the central role of consent in all sexual activities, including in those Member States that still require the use of force or threat in their legislation. This provision is an important step towards promoting a change in social and cultural patterns of behaviour and ultimately reducing the prevalence of rape in the EU.

The Commission will work closely with Member States to ensure that this provision is transposed and implemented correctly. It will continue to share best practices in the area of violence against women through its Mutual Learning Programme2 as well as the new European Network on the prevention of gender-based violence.
1 The Proposal for this Directive can be found here: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-

content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52022PC0105. The final text has not been published on the date of this writing. The article on consent was not included in the original Proposal but added later on by the co-legislators. 2 Mutual learning Programme in gender equality: https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-andpolicy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/gender-equality/who-we-work-gender-equality/mutual-learningprogramme-gender-equality_en
